The Russian Federation makes a considerable contribution to the implementation of the provisions of the convention and its protocols, including in demining activities and in clearing land from any explosive devices within its own territory as well as abroad. Mr. President, Brazil attaches particular importance to the universalization of the Convention and its protocols. Universal adherence strengthens not only their legal authority, but also their practical capacity to protect civilians and combatants from weapons that may cause unnecessary suffering or have indiscriminate effects. Brazil also recognizes the valuable contribution of the sponsorship program. Broad and geographically representative participation is essential to the legitimacy and effectiveness of the Convention. We encourage states in a position to do so to continue supporting the program. Compliance and national implementation are equally fundamental. The effectiveness of the CCW ultimately depends upon the implementation of its obligations at the national level. Brazil therefore supports efforts to improve compliance reporting, enhance awareness about the convention and its protocols among armed forces and civilian populations, and strengthen international cooperation and assistance. At the same time, we cannot overlook the difficulties that have affected the functioning of the Convention in recent years. Procedural disagreements have prevented High Contracting Parties from conducting substantive discussions in the formal meetings of the CCW for three consecutive years. This situation should concern us all. While procedural questions deserve appropriate consideration, they should not prevent the Convention from carrying out its substantive work or undermine its ability to respond to the humanitarian challenges within its mandate. As is widely known, the meetings of the follow-up process of the Convention have traditionally taken decisions by consensus. This is not a rule, but a tradition. The tradition has helped ensure that the Convention enjoys universal support by its high contracting parties and has contributed to enhance its implementation. But it cannot be misconstrued as a veto power, and it cannot continue to serve as a vehicle for institutional paralysis. This risks undermining the Convention and putting its relevance in question. Mr. President, in view of this, my delegation will support your efforts to overcome the procedural impasses that have prevented substantive debates in the meetings of the Convention in previous years, and we trust that these efforts will enable the Review Conference to achieve a successful outcome and lay the basis for an effective review cycle in the upcoming five-year period. I thank you, Mr. President.

I thank the distinguished representative of Panama. I give the floor to observers at this stage, namely Mart for peace. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chairperson. We all know that international humanitarian law imposes restrictions on the use of incendiary weapons, given the physical and psychological suffering they cause to victims, such as severe burns and respiratory damage. The Third Protocol to the Convention prohibits the use of airdropped incendiary weapons against civilians, but there are two legal loopholes that hinder the protection of civilians. First, the protocol's definition excludes certain multipurpose munitions, notably white phosphorus, which are not primarily designed to start fires or burn people, although they can cause similar effects. Second, the protocol differentiates between the means of delivery of these weapons, as it prohibits the use of airdropped incendiary weapons against civilian populations. But there are fewer restrictions on ground launched incendiary weapons, even though the effects of burns and destruction do not differ depending on the delivery method. Matt has documented the use of white phosphorus in several armed conflicts, including in the Gaza Strip, as well as artillery shells that exploded in the air, causing serious harms to civilians. We have also documented the damage caused by the use of ground-launched incendiary weapons in Ukraine. These facts raise serious concerns about the adequacy of the Third Protocol in achieving its goal of protecting civilians, due to its failure to explicitly condemn certain multipurpose weapons, such as white phosphorus. Furthermore, it contains weaker regulations for ground-launched incendiary weapons compared to those dropped from the air, even though all these weapons produce the same damage. Therefore, MATT recommends the urgent initiation of informal discussions regarding the adequacy of international law concerning incendiary weapons and the concerns raised by these weapons. It is also essential to work towards developing stronger international standards for better protection of civilians to address the gaps in the Third Protocol. I thank you.
